transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-14 15:00 UTC | Duration: 40m | Recorded (Fireflies)
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE); Priya Nair (Redwood SE); Laura Kim (Vertex CTO); Ethan Morales (Lead Eng); Ravi Shah (Product); Maya Lin (Security)

Summary: quick hosted API demo covering chat and text generation basics — streaming, key params (temperature, max_tokens, top_p), retries and idempotency, and common enterprise questions around data retention and KMS. Customer interested in doing a short pilot to validate latency/cost for a patient triage feature.

Topics: intro, current infra & constraints, demo walkthrough (console + API), streaming response options, rate limits/retries/backoff, security & compliance, next steps

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, and with me is Priya from our Solutions Engineering team. How are you all doing?
[00:09] Laura: Doing well, thanks. We're excited to see what you've got — been looking at a few providers so want to see how Redwood stacks for production.
[00:15] Alex: Great — quick agenda: a 20-ish minute demo of the Hosted API for chat/text generation, touch on streaming and parameters, then Priya will go into a couple of technical details around retries and deployment options. We'll leave time for questions and next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Ethan: Yep. For context, we're building an automated patient triage assistant — mostly text generation with follow-up clarifications. Key constraints: sub-300ms p50 latency for short prompts, predictable cost, and SOC2 compliance.
[00:40] Priya: Got it. A couple clarifying q's: are you planning synchronous API calls from the app, or more of an async job queue with worker pools?
[00:48] Ravi: Mostly synchronous from the mobile app, but we can add server-side caching for common prefixes. We want streaming so the UI feels snappy.
[00:56] Priya: Streaming's good for UX. Redwood's hosted API supports streaming via SSE and chunked HTTP. We'll demo the console streaming first, then show an SDK example.
[01:10] Alex: Also, quick note on model choices — we have curated open models and Redwood-verified profiles; you can pick a lower-cost variant if you need to trade off a bit of quality for latency.
[01:22] Maya: From security — what happens to PII in requests? Is it retained? We need details on retention and KMS.
[01:29] Alex: Short answer: hosted keeps short-term logs for debugging by default, but you can opt out of retention or enable customer-managed keys through our KMS integration. We'll share the SOC2 and KMS docs in the security follow-up.
[01:42] Priya: Ok jumping into the console — screen share shows the Hosted API page, model catalog, and a sample chat playground. Note: our streaming toggle is here, you can also choose chunked vs SSE for different client implementations.
[01:58] [01:58] Priya (continues): I'll run a quick example prompt: "Patient reports chest pain and shortness of breath, what triage steps would you recommend?" I'll use the default profile, temperature 0.2, max_tokens 250, top_p 0.95.
[02:15] [02:15] System synth voice: (auto-transcription) "Streaming response starting..."
[02:20] Priya: You can see tokens arrive progressively — this reduces perceived latency because UI can render partial replies. For our mobile app, chunked HTTP was simpler to implement in the webview, SSE works well for single-page apps.
[02:36] Ethan: For mobile, what's the recommended chunk size or buffer? Any best practices?
[02:41] Priya: We recommend smaller chunks for chat (200-500 ms intervals) and limit each chunk to a few hundred tokens. Redwood's runtime batches requests under the hood so you won't get tiny tokenized overheads.
[02:55] Alex: On params: temp controls randomness, top_p is nucleus sampling, max_tokens caps output length. For deterministic outputs use temp 0 or lower top_p. You can also pin model versions to avoid drift.
[03:10] Ravi: How do retries work? If we get a 5xx, should we retry client-side? What's your guidance to avoid duplicate side-effects?
[03:18] Priya: Good q. We recommend idempotency keys for POST-like generation requests that create side effects. For transient errors, exponential backoff with jitter is recommended. Redwood supports idempotency headers and will deduplicate requests for a short window — we'll include SDK snippets.
[03:34] Laura: Any rate limiting / quotas? We need to understand throttling and burst behavior for peak times.
[03:39] Alex: Hosted tier has per-account rate limits and burst windows; we surface limits in the dashboard and you can request quota uplifts. For Dedicated you'd get reserved capacity and predictable throughput.
[03:50] Priya: Now a quick look at the API — here's a POST to /v1/chat with messages array. We'll toggle stream=true to show server-sent events. Example: {
  model: "redwood-chat-small-v1",
  messages: [...],
  temperature:0.2, max_tokens:250, stream:true
}
[04:12] [04:12] Priya: The stream frames include partial deltas and a final done event. If the client disconnects, you can re-open with an idempotency key to pick up, depending on your pattern.
[04:22] Ethan: Is the streaming protocol compatible with our existing SSE library?
[04:25] Priya: Yes — SSE or chunked both compatible. We also have SDK helpers that surface an async iterator for streaming tokens.
[04:33] Ravi: How about retries + streaming — if stream breaks mid-response, is there a way to resume?
[04:38] Priya: Not a byte-level resume, but you can re-request with the last partial output as context and an idempotency key; depending on model deterministic behavior may vary. For critical flows we recommend short responses with incremental prompts so replays are cheap.
[04:55] Alex: On observability — Redwood Console shows token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, and tail latency alerts. That helps you decide when to switch to a lower-latency model or enable caching.
[05:10] Maya: For compliance we need logs for audit — will those be redacted automatically?
[05:16] Alex: We support configurable redaction and audit logs; by default PII in logs is not automatically redacted, but you can enable redaction rules or forward logs to your SIEM via our log sink. We'll send the security doc.
[05:29] Ethan: Performance: you mentioned p50 under 300ms — is that realistic on hosted for a 128-token prompt?
[05:36] Priya: For short prompts and optimized models yes, p50 can be sub-300ms on supported regions; p90 will be higher. We can run a pilot benchmark to show real numbers for your prompt shapes.
[05:48] Laura: Cost — how do you measure? Token-based billing? Any overage rules?
[05:54] Alex: Hosted is token-based for generation and per-embedding unit for embeddings. The Console gives token breakdowns and estimated monthly cost. For big usage we recommend Dedicated commits to lower unit costs.
[06:06] Ravi: Any concerns about hallucinations in clinical subject matter? Do you recommend a reranking or retrieval augmentation?
[06:12] Priya: For clinical you should couple generation with a retrieval step — retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) or structured prompts and a verification pass. We also support tool-calling and function outputs to keep answers structured.
[06:26] [06:26] Priya: Quick demo of SDK snippet (node): show code that streams tokens and does exponential backoff on 5xx. Code example includes idempotency-key header.
[06:38] Alex: A couple of common gotchas: 1) big batch sizes can increase latency due to batching window; 2) quantized model variants reduce memory and cost but may change quality; 3) caching prefix responses reduces cost for repeat questions.
[06:57] Ethan: For caching, do you support prefix/KV cache or is that on our side?
[07:02] Priya: Redwood has automatic prefix caching at the runtime level for repeated prefixes across requests — it's on by default where safe. You can also implement app-level caches.
[07:12] Ravi: If we want no retention for HIPAA reasons, can you do that on hosted?
[07:17] Maya: HIPAA needs BAAs normally — do you have that?
[07:20] Alex: We do enterprise agreements and can support BAAs in Private/Dedicated modes; for Hosted we have options to disable retention and enable customer-managed encryption but talk to sales for the contract. We'll mark that as a security follow-up.
[07:35] [07:35] Priya: Back to retries — recommended pattern: client retries on 429 with backoff; for 5xx use short exponential backoff and only retry idempotent requests. Use idempotency keys for user-visible side effects.
[07:51] Ethan: Any circuit-breaker guidance?
[07:53] Priya: Yes — implement retry budgets and circuit breakers; the Console can alert you and we expose error-rate dashboards.
[07:59] Laura: Want to map next steps: we'll run a 1-week pilot, share volumes, Redwood will provide pricing and benchmark plan, security follow-up.
[08:09] Alex: Perfect. I'll send the hosted pricing deck and a pilot onboarding doc. Priya will give the SDK snippets and benchmark spreadsheet.
[08:17] [08:17] Ravi: One last question — model rollouts and version pinning?
[08:20] Priya: You can pin a model version in deployment config. Rollouts support canary and A/B via the Console so you can test new variants gradually. If a new model shows regressions you can automatically fallback to the previous variant.
[08:34] [08:34] Laura: Ok great thanks — that helps.
[08:36] Alex: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the items.
[08:39] [08:39] End of recording.
